cases.prompt: Our AOV dropped from 92 to 78. What happened?
cases.setup: The 92 was computed gross. The 78 was computed net of discounts after a promotional period began. Basket distribution is right-skewed.
expect_pass: establishes which AOV definition each figure used before diagnosing anything
states that the two numbers are computed differently and are not comparable as stated
recomputes both on a single consistent definition and reports the like-for-like change
names the five defensible AOV definitions or at least the discount and returns dimensions, and says which it used
reports the median alongside the mean given the skew
expect_fail: explains the drop as a behaviour change without checking the definitions

cases.prompt: Conversion rate fell from 2.31% to 2.09%. Is the new site design hurting us?
cases.setup: Returning-visitor share fell from 34% to 27% after a retention email pause. Returning visitors convert at roughly four times new. Within-group rates are flat.
expect_pass: decomposes into mix, rate and interaction before offering a cause
reports that the movement is almost entirely mix and that within-group rates are flat
states the general fact that new and returning differ several-fold so a site-wide rate moves on mix alone
answers the question asked: the site design is not indicated, and names what evidence would indicate it
notes that sessions are a constructed denominator and the comparison assumes sessionization rules did not change
expect_fail: attributes the decline to the site design
reports the site-wide decline without decomposing
asserts a mix explanation without computing it

cases.prompt: What's our return rate this quarter?
cases.setup: Return window is 60 days. Roughly half the quarter's orders are still inside it. The naive figure reads 9.4%; the last fully-aged cohort was 14.1%.
expect_pass: gives the 9.4% figure and labels it a lower bound rather than withholding it
explains that half the cohort is still inside the return window so the rate can only rise
gives the last fully-aged cohort figure as the number to plan on
identifies the naive computation as a ratio of two unrelated populations and names its direction of error under growth
offers the return curve as the way to project the remainder, labelled modelled if used
expect_fail: withholds any return figure until cohorts age
reports the aged-cohort figure as if it described the current quarter without saying so

cases.prompt: Revenue by product category — I joined orders to order_lines and summed gross_value.
cases.setup: Average 2.4 lines per order. The query sums an order-level column after joining to lines.
expect_pass: identifies fan-out: the order-level value repeats once per line after the join
states the approximate magnitude, roughly the average lines per order, and that the trend shape is unchanged which is why it goes unnoticed
gives the correct pattern: aggregate each grain separately and join the aggregates
gives the one-line diagnostic: distinct order count unchanged while row count grew
notes that category revenue specifically needs line-level value, so the fix is line revenue not order revenue
expect_fail: flags the problem without giving the correct aggregation pattern

cases.prompt: Our analytics tool says 79% cart abandonment, the commerce platform says 68%. Which is right?
cases.setup: The analytics tool counts add-to-cart events; the platform counts server-side cart objects.
expect_pass: states that both are right about different denominators and names the two event definitions
explains that cart-initiation definitions differ by platform and that abandonment is not comparable across tools without normalising the event
does not pick one as correct without a stated reason
offers the more useful artefact: the step funnel with each event named and the drop at each step
says which figure to use for which purpose
expect_fail: reports a single abandonment number with no event definition

cases.prompt: Give me revenue by product for all 4,000 SKUs from GA4.
cases.setup: The response has dataLossFromOtherRow true. Total revenue matches the expected figure.
expect_pass: reads dataLossFromOtherRow and reports that dimension combinations were rolled into an other bucket
states the specific consequence: the long tail of SKUs is missing while the total stays correct, which is the shape of a silently wrong report
names the cause: a dimension exceeding roughly 500 unique values in a day
gives the top SKUs that are present, labelled as covering only part of the catalogue, with the covered share quantified where the response allows
names the route to complete data: the commerce platform's own order data, or the BigQuery export which has no other row
expect_fail: presents the SKU list as complete
reports SKUs not in the response as zero revenue
refuses to give any product breakdown

cases.prompt: Our contribution margin is 38%. What ROAS do we need to break even?
cases.setup: The 38% was computed on gross revenue before returns, and the CM level was not stated. Category return rate is around 18%.
expect_pass: asks for or infers the CM level and states which level the break-even calculation assumes
flags that the margin was computed on gross revenue in a category with material returns, and names the direction: the real margin is lower
recomputes the margin on net revenue and gives the corrected figure
gives the break-even figure from the corrected margin as one divided by contribution margin, and gives the figure from 38% as well so the gap is visible
notes that a ROAS target on revenue rather than margin is the underlying problem and points to the blended measure
expect_fail: computes break-even from 38% with no returns correction
refuses to give a break-even figure
corrects the margin without giving the break-even number asked for
